description_ru: Аукцион невостребованного багажа на вокзале, чемодан без хозяина и покупатель, который находит внутри куда больше, чем рассчитывал. Лёгкая загадочная история с иронией.
text:
Every spring, the railway company cleared its cellar of the things that people had left behind, and every spring a small and peculiar congregation gathered to buy them. They assembled in the old parcel office at Kessling Junction, a long room with a high ceiling and a smell of cold iron, and they sat on folding chairs facing a trestle table with the guarded expressions of poker players at a christening.

There were the professionals: dealers in curiosities with pockets full of loupes and the gleam of the perpetually optimistic. There were the amateurs, who had seen a television programme and believed that every battered suitcase contained a Fabergé egg. And there was, always, Cornelius Bray, a retired schoolmaster who attended every year, bought exactly one lot, and refused to explain why.

The auctioneer, a stout man named Mr. Tolliver with a voice like gravel in a bucket, conducted the proceedings with the weary brio of a man who had sold ten thousand umbrellas. "Lot thirty-nine, gentlemen. One set of golf clubs, minus two clubs and any sense of dignity. Who'll give me five pounds?" A wave of laughter, a nod, a sale. The afternoon unfolded with its usual lumbering absurdity: a stuffed pike, a trombone, a crate of left-handed scissors, and a wedding dress in a bin liner which fetched, to the consternation of everyone, forty pounds.

Cornelius sat at the back, with his hat on his knee and his old wool coat buttoned to the chin, bidding for nothing. He had a method. He did not examine the lots; he merely watched, with the quiet, unhurried attention of a man bird-watching, and waited for the one that spoke to him.

At a quarter to four, Mr. Tolliver lifted from the floor a battered leather case, tied around its middle with a belt. It was the colour of strong tea and covered in the faded ghosts of labels from places that no longer existed under those names. "Lot forty-seven," he said. "Unclaimed since, well, the ledger says nineteen seventy-one, and I wouldn't dispute it. Contents unknown. Lock defeated, by the look of it, by somebody with a grudge. Shall we say ten pounds?"

Nobody moved. It looked heavy, and heaviness in unclaimed luggage generally signifies bricks, or bad news. Cornelius, however, felt the old, inexplicable tug, as of a fish taking the line. He raised one finger a quarter of an inch. "Ten pounds, the gentleman at the back. Any advance? No? Sold, and may God have mercy on your hallway."

He took the case home on the bus, holding it on his lap like a sleeping child, and when he had put the kettle on and arranged himself in the armchair, he undid the belt. Inside, folded with the precision of a person who expects to return, were three shirts, a razor in a leather pouch, and a tin of boiled sweets that had long since fused into a single amber brick. Beneath these lay a bundle of letters, tied with green ribbon, and a small, flat notebook bound in black cloth.

He read the notebook first. It was, he realised after the first page, a travel diary, written in a small and fastidious hand by a man named Arthur Penhallow, who had been on his way to the coast in the autumn of 1971 to meet a woman. The prose was dry, observant and ridiculously funny. Arthur described his fellow passengers with the cruelty of a naturalist: a vicar who slept with his mouth open in the manner of a startled haddock, a child who ate a sandwich in six distinct and logical stages. He confessed, in the last entry, to a stomach full of nerves. "I have rehearsed what I will say for four hundred miles," he wrote, "and I have discovered that every version is worse than silence. I think I shall simply stand there and be extremely glad."

The entry stopped there, in mid-afternoon, at a station called Kessling Junction, where the train had stopped for twelve minutes. Cornelius turned the page. It was blank. He turned another. Blank. He sat for a long time with the notebook open on his knee, and the kettle began to scream, and he did not hear it.

Then he opened the letters. They were all addressed to the same woman, Margery Holloway, at a seaside address, and they had all been written but never posted. There were nineteen of them. They were, he concluded after a decent interval of shame and then of fascination, the most patient love letters ever composed by a man who could not say anything to a woman's face, and they ended, quite abruptly, in the autumn of 1971.

Cornelius was a schoolmaster, and schoolmasters have a deep, perverse faith in follow-up. The next morning he went to the library and, with the dogged stubbornness of the retired, began to investigate. It took him three weeks, a great many microfilms, and one memorable altercation with an archivist. He discovered that Arthur Penhallow had left the train at Kessling to buy a newspaper, had been unexpectedly detained by a collapsed bridge up the line, and had spent the night in a waiting room. By the time he reached the coast, the case had been lost, and with it the letters, the address, and the courage. Margery Holloway had waited on the platform at the other end for four hours, and then gone home.

But she had not, it transpired, gone far. At the age of eighty-one, she lived in a small bungalow twelve miles from the sea, a sharp-eyed woman with a parrot and a deep distrust of men with clipboards. When Cornelius knocked on her door, case in hand, she looked at him, then at the leather, and said, in a voice like dry paper, "Well. You took your time." "I am so sorry," said Cornelius. "It was in a cellar." "Most things are," said Margery.

She read the letters that evening, all nineteen, while Cornelius sat in the kitchen with the parrot and a cup of tea that had gone cold. When she came to find him, her eyes were red, and her expression was that of a person who has been handed a vast and unexpected inheritance in a currency that no longer exists.

"He was a ridiculous man," she said. "He married a dentist in the end. I went to the wedding, out of spite." "And?"

"And I was extremely glad," said Margery Holloway, and she smiled, slowly, like a sunrise reconsidering.

questions.question: Where did the auction take place?
questions.answer: In the old parcel office at Kessling Junction.

questions.question: What did Cornelius find inside the case?
questions.answer: Shirts, a razor, a tin of sweets, letters and a travel diary.

questions.question: Why were the love letters never posted?
questions.answer: The case was lost after Arthur's journey was disrupted.

questions.question: How did the story end?
questions.answer: Cornelius returned the letters to Margery, who was glad.
